claim: Salmonella is a major foodborne pathogen that can effectively replicate inside host macrophages to establish life-threatening systemic infections.
source: Salmonella is a major foodborne pathogen that can effectively replicate inside host macrophages to establish life-threatening systemic infections.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the scientific literature about Salmonella pathogenesis.

claim: An estimated 93.8 million cases of gastroenteritis and 27 million cases of systemic diseases caused by Salmonella species occur annually worldwide, with 355,000 deaths.
source: An estimated 93.8 million cases of gastroenteritis and 27 million cases of systemic diseases caused by Salmonella species occur annually worldwide, with 355,000 deaths (Kim et al., 2019; Majowicz et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2019 and Majowicz et al., 2010.

claim: The ability to survive and replicate in host macrophages is a key determinant for Salmonella to induce systemic infection.
source: The ability to survive and replicate in host macrophages is a key determinant for Salmonella to induce systemic infection (Fields et al., 1986; LaRock et al., 2015; Leung and Finlay, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fields et al., 1986; LaRock et al., 2015; and Leung and Finlay, 1991.

claim: After internalization by macrophages, Salmonella delivers a set of more than 30 effector proteins to the macrophage cytoplasm, mainly through a type III secretion system (T3SS) encoded by Salmonella pathogenicity island-2 (SPI-2).
source: After internalization by macrophages, Salmonella delivers a set of more than 30 effector proteins to the macrophage cytoplasm, mainly through a type III secretion system (T3SS) encoded by Salmonella pathogenicity island-2 (SPI-2) (Pillay et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pillay et al., 2023.

claim: SPI-2 effectors manipulate diverse cellular processes to promote the formation of a membrane-bound compartment, termed the Salmonella-containing vacuole (SCV), a niche where Salmonella resides and grows.
source: SPI-2 effectors manipulate diverse cellular processes to promote the formation of a membrane-bound compartment, termed the Salmonella-containing vacuole (SCV), a niche where Salmonella resides and grows (Castanheira and García-del Portillo, 2017; Rosenberg et al., 2022; Steeb et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Castanheira and García-del Portillo, 2017; Rosenberg et al., 2022; and Steeb et al., 2013.

claim: SCV protects Salmonella from contact with antimicrobial agents in macrophages.
source: SCV protects Salmonella from contact with antimicrobial agents in macrophages (Figueira and Holden, 2012; Li et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Figueira and Holden, 2012 and Li et al., 2023.

claim: SPI-2 effectors induce the formation of specific tubular membrane compartments that extend from the SCV, known as Salmonella-induced filaments (SIFs).
source: Moreover, SPI-2 effectors induce the formation of specific tubular membrane compartments that extend from the SCV, known as Salmonella-induced filaments (SIFs).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: SIFs allow Salmonella to access various types of endocytosed nutrients, thereby facilitating efficient replication within macrophages.
source: These filaments allow Salmonella to access various types of endocytosed nutrients, thereby facilitating efficient replication within macrophages (Brumell et al., 2001; Liss et al., 2017; Rajashekar et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brumell et al., 2001; Liss et al., 2017; and Rajashekar et al., 2008.

claim: The SCV of macrophages is a nutrient-poor environment.
source: As the SCV of macrophages is a nutrient-poor environment (Fields et al., 1986; Kehl et al., 2020), to effectively replicate in the SCV, Salmonella needs to acquire a wide range of host nutrients or host-derived metabolites and synthesize metabolites de novo that cannot be sufficiently accessed from the host (Dandekar et al., 2014; Röder et al., 2021; Tuli and Sharma, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fields et al., 1986 and Kehl et al., 2020.

claim: To effectively replicate in the SCV, Salmonella needs to acquire a wide range of host nutrients or host-derived metabolites and synthesize metabolites de novo that cannot be sufficiently accessed from the host.
source: As the SCV of macrophages is a nutrient-poor environment (Fields et al., 1986; Kehl et al., 2020), to effectively replicate in the SCV, Salmonella needs to acquire a wide range of host nutrients or host-derived metabolites and synthesize metabolites de novo that cannot be sufficiently accessed from the host (Dandekar et al., 2014; Röder et al., 2021; Tuli and Sharma, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dandekar et al., 2014; Röder et al., 2021; and Tuli and Sharma, 2019.

claim: Nutrients/metabolites are used by intracellular Salmonella either as carbon sources to generate energy or for the synthesis of fatty acids and proteins.
source: Nutrients/metabolites are used by intracellular Salmonella either as carbon sources to generate energy or for the synthesis of fatty acids and proteins (Dandekar et al., 2014; Steeb et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dandekar et al., 2014 and Steeb et al., 2013.

claim: Several metabolites were found to be employed by Salmonella as environmental cues to induce the expression of virulence genes.
source: Moreover, several metabolites were found to be employed by Salmonella as environmental cues to induce the expression of virulence genes (Jiang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2021 and Wang et al., 2023.

claim: β-Alanine is the only naturally occurring β-type amino acid and is found in all living organisms.
source: β-Alanine, also known as 3-aminopropionic acid (3-AP), is the only naturally occurring β-type amino acid and is found in all living organisms (Song et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Song et al., 2023.

claim: β-Alanine can be synthesized de novo by bacteria, fungi, and plants.
source: β-Alanine can be synthesized de novo by bacteria, fungi, and plants, whereas animals need to obtain it from food or generate it via the catabolism of cytosine and uracil (Gojković et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gojković et al., 2001 and Wang et al., 2021b.

claim: Animals need to obtain β-alanine from food or generate it via the catabolism of cytosine and uracil.
source: β-Alanine can be synthesized de novo by bacteria, fungi, and plants, whereas animals need to obtain it from food or generate it via the catabolism of cytosine and uracil (Gojković et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gojković et al., 2001 and Wang et al., 2021b.

claim: In bacteria, β-alanine is synthesized via the decarboxylation of L-aspartate, a reaction catalyzed by L-aspartate decarboxylase (PanD).
source: In bacteria, β-alanine is synthesized via the decarboxylation of L-aspartate, a reaction catalyzed by L-aspartate decarboxylase (PanD) (Begley et al., 2001; Schmitzberger et al., 2003; West et al., 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Begley et al., 2001; Schmitzberger et al., 2003; and West et al., 1985.

claim: The panD gene is conserved among most bacteria.
source: The panD gene is conserved among most bacteria (Nozaki et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nozaki et al., 2012.

claim: β-alanine forms a part of pantothenate (vitamin B5), which is the key precursor for the biosynthesis of coenzyme A (CoA).
source: First, β-alanine forms a part of pantothenate (vitamin B5), which is the key precursor for the biosynthesis of coenzyme A (CoA) (Webb et al., 2004; White et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Webb et al., 2004 and White et al., 2001.

claim: CoA is an essential cofactor involved in many metabolic pathways, including the synthesis and degradation of fatty acids, pyruvate oxidation through the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and the production of secondary metabolites.
source: CoA is an essential cofactor involved in many metabolic pathways, including the synthesis and degradation of fatty acids, pyruvate oxidation through the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and the production of secondary metabolites (Davaapil et al., 2014; Gout, 2019; Sibon and Strauss, 2016; Theodoulou et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Davaapil et al., 2014; Gout, 2019; Sibon and Strauss, 2016; and Theodoulou et al., 2014.

claim: β-alanine is a limiting precursor of carnosine, a nonenzymatic free radical scavenger and a natural antioxidant, with anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects in animals.
source: Second, β-alanine is a limiting precursor of carnosine, a nonenzymatic free radical scavenger and a natural antioxidant, with anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects in animals (Boldyrev et al., 2013; Hoffman et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boldyrev et al., 2013 and Hoffman et al., 2018.

claim: In the past 15 years, β-alanine has become one of the most commonly used sports supplements worldwide.
source: In the past 15 y, β-alanine has become one of the most commonly used sports supplements worldwide (Bellinger, 2014; Hoffman et al., 2018; Huerta Ojeda, Tapia Huerta Ojeda et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bellinger, 2014; Hoffman et al., 2018; and Huerta Ojeda, Tapia Huerta Ojeda et al., 2020.

claim: A total of 26 free amino acids were analyzed in the targeted metabolomics study.
source: A total of 26 free amino acids were analyzed, and eight showed significant differences in abundance between the two groups (VIP (Variable Importance in the Projection) >1 and p<0.05; FC (fold change) > 1.5 or < 0.667) (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text describing the metabolomics analysis.

claim: Eight amino acids showed significant differences in abundance between mock-infected and Salmonella-infected macrophages.
source: A total of 26 free amino acids were analyzed, and eight showed significant differences in abundance between the two groups (VIP (Variable Importance in the Projection) >1 and p<0.05; FC (fold change) > 1.5 or < 0.667) (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1C and D and described in the text.

claim: The concentrations of L-hydroxyproline, L-citrulline and L-cysteine were upregulated in Salmonella-infected macrophages compared to mock-infected macrophages.
source: Compared with those in the mock-infected group, the concentrations of three amino acids (L-hydroxyproline, L-citrulline and L-cysteine) were upregulated (Figure 1C), and five amino acids (L-asparagine, L-serine, L-aspartate, β-alanine and γ-aminobutyric acid) were downregulated (Figure 1D) in the Salmonella-infected group.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1C and described in the text.

claim: The concentrations of L-asparagine, L-serine, L-aspartate, β-alanine and γ-aminobutyric acid were downregulated in Salmonella-infected macrophages compared to mock-infected macrophages.
source: Compared with those in the mock-infected group, the concentrations of three amino acids (L-hydroxyproline, L-citrulline and L-cysteine) were upregulated (Figure 1C), and five amino acids (L-asparagine, L-serine, L-aspartate, β-alanine and γ-aminobutyric acid) were downregulated (Figure 1D) in the Salmonella-infected group.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1D and described in the text.

claim: Intracellular serine concentrations were downregulated due to the reprogramming of macrophage glucose metabolism during Salmonella infection.
source: Consistent with previous findings, intracellular serine concentrations were downregulated due to the reprogramming of macrophage glucose metabolism during Salmonella infection (Jiang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2021 and is consistent with the data presented.

claim: Salmonella can use host-derived aspartate and asparagine for growth in macrophages.
source: Salmonella can use host-derived aspartate and asparagine for growth in macrophages (Popp et al., 2015); therefore, the decrease in intracellular aspartate and asparagine upon Salmonella infection is likely due to their utilization by bacteria.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Popp et al., 2015.

claim: The decrease in intracellular aspartate and asparagine upon Salmonella infection is likely due to their utilization by bacteria.
source: Salmonella can use host-derived aspartate and asparagine for growth in macrophages (Popp et al., 2015); therefore, the decrease in intracellular aspartate and asparagine upon Salmonella infection is likely due to their utilization by bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the citation and the observed data.

claim: β-alanine concentrations were downregulated in Salmonella-infected macrophages.
source: Interestingly, β-alanine concentrations were also downregulated in the Salmonella-infected group (Figure 1D), suggesting that intracellular Salmonella may use host-derived β-alanine for growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Intracellular Salmonella may use host-derived β-alanine for growth.
source: Interestingly, β-alanine concentrations were also downregulated in the Salmonella-infected group (Figure 1D), suggesting that intracellular Salmonella may use host-derived β-alanine for growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decrease in β-alanine levels.

claim: The replication of Salmonella in RAW264.7 cells significantly increased with the addition of 1, 2, or 4 mM β-alanine.
source: The results showed that the replication of Salmonella in RAW264.7 cells significantly (p<0.001) increased with the addition of 1, 2, or 4 mM β-alanine (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: β-alanine enhanced Salmonella intracellular replication in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, β-alanine enhanced Salmonella intracellular replication in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Host-derived β-alanine facilitates Salmonella replication inside macrophages.
source: The results suggest that host-derived β-alanine facilitates Salmonella replication inside macrophages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased replication with β-alanine addition.

claim: The addition of 1 mM β-alanine did not influence the ROS and RNS levels in Salmonella-infected RAW264.7 cells.
source: We observed that the addition of 1 mM β-alanine did not influence the ROS (reactive oxygen species) and RNS (reactive nitrogen species) levels in Salmonella-infected RAW264.7 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of 1 mM β-alanine did not affect the percentage of pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages (CD86+) and anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages (CD163+) during Salmonella infection.
source: Flow cytometry analysis indicated that the addition of 1 mM β-alanine did not affect the percentage of pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages (CD86+) and anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages (CD163+) during Salmonella infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), implying that the addition of β-alanine to macrophages does not change their immune response.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The addition of β-alanine to macrophages does not change their immune response.
source: Flow cytometry analysis indicated that the addition of 1 mM β-alanine did not affect the percentage of pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages (CD86+) and anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages (CD163+) during Salmonella infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), implying that the addition of β-alanine to macrophages does not change their immune response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the flow cytometry data.

claim: Salmonella use host-derived β-alanine for intracellular growth.
source: Combining these results, we can further infer that Salmonella use host-derived β-alanine for intracellular growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental results.

claim: Escherichia coli uptakes β-alanine via the transporter protein CycA.
source: Escherichia coli uptakes β-alanine via the transporter protein CycA (Schneider et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schneider et al., 2004.

claim: The Salmonella ΔcycA mutant was able to use β-alanine as the sole carbon source for growth in minimal medium.
source: However, the Salmonella ΔcycA mutant was able to use β-alanine as the sole carbon source for growth in minimal medium (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4), indicating that CycA is not a transporter for β-alanine in Salmonella.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: CycA is not a transporter for β-alanine in Salmonella.
source: However, the Salmonella ΔcycA mutant was able to use β-alanine as the sole carbon source for growth in minimal medium (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4), indicating that CycA is not a transporter for β-alanine in Salmonella.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that the ΔcycA mutant can still use β-alanine.

claim: Mutation of cycA did not influence the replication of Salmonella in RAW264.7 cells.
source: Consistent with these results, mutation of cycA did not influence the replication of Salmonella in RAW264.7 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) or colonization in mouse systemic tissues (liver and spleen; Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Mutation of cycA did not influence colonization in mouse systemic tissues (liver and spleen).
source: Consistent with these results, mutation of cycA did not influence the replication of Salmonella in RAW264.7 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) or colonization in mouse systemic tissues (liver and spleen; Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: In E. coli, GabP transports γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a structural analog of β-alanine, and may also transport β-alanine.
source: In E. coli, GabP transports γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a structural analog of β-alanine, and may also transport β-alanine (Pavić et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pavić et al., 2021.

claim: The Salmonella ∆gabP mutant displayed no growth defect in minimal medium with β-alanine as the sole carbon source.
source: Nevertheless, the Salmonella ∆gabP mutant displayed no growth defect in minimal medium with β-alanine as the sole carbon source (Figure 1—figure supplements 7 and 8), indicating that GabP is not involved in β-alanine uptake in Salmonella.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplements 7 and 8.

claim: GabP is not involved in β-alanine uptake in Salmonella.
source: Nevertheless, the Salmonella ∆gabP mutant displayed no growth defect in minimal medium with β-alanine as the sole carbon source (Figure 1—figure supplements 7 and 8), indicating that GabP is not involved in β-alanine uptake in Salmonella.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that the ∆gabP mutant can still use β-alanine.

claim: The ΔargT mutant showed markedly decreased growth in the minimal medium with β-alanine as the sole carbon source.
source: Strikingly, the ΔargT mutant—defective in arginine uptake—showed markedly decreased growth in the minimal medium with β-alanine as the sole carbon source (Figure 1F), suggesting that ArgT also transports β-alanine in Salmonella.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: ArgT also transports β-alanine in Salmonella.
source: Strikingly, the ΔargT mutant—defective in arginine uptake—showed markedly decreased growth in the minimal medium with β-alanine as the sole carbon source (Figure 1F), suggesting that ArgT also transports β-alanine in Salmonella.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing decreased growth of the ΔargT mutant with β-alanine.

claim: ArgT is essential for Salmonella replication within macrophages and full virulence in vivo.
source: It has been reported that ArgT is essential for Salmonella replication within macrophages and full virulence in vivo (Das et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Das et al., 2010.

claim: The decarboxylation of L-aspartate to β-alanine is the rate-limiting step of β-alanine generation.
source: Salmonella can de novo synthesize β-alanine via the decarboxylation of L-aspartate, which is catalyzed by L-aspartate decarboxylase (PanD) (Figure 2A) and is reportedly the rate-limiting step of β-alanine generation (Begley et al., 2001; Schmitzberger et al., 2003; West et al., 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Begley et al., 2001; Schmitzberger et al., 2003; and West et al., 1985.

claim: The expression level of panD was significantly greater in RAW264.7 cells than in RPMI-1640 medium.
source: Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT‒PCR) assays revealed that the expression level of panD was significantly (p<0.01) greater in RAW264.7 cells than in RPMI-1640 medium (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Increased expression of panD was observed in N-minimal medium.
source: Increased expression of panD was also observed in N-minimal medium, a widely used medium that mimics the conditions inside macrophages, as revealed by qRT‒PCR and bioluminescent reporter assays (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C and D.

claim: panD expression is enhanced during Salmonella growth inside macrophages.
source: These results demonstrate that panD expression is enhanced during Salmonella growth inside macrophages, suggesting a relationship between panD expression and intracellular Salmonella growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the qRT-PCR and bioluminescent reporter assay data.

claim: There is a relationship between panD expression and intracellular Salmonella growth.
source: These results demonstrate that panD expression is enhanced during Salmonella growth inside macrophages, suggesting a relationship between panD expression and intracellular Salmonella growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increased expression of panD in macrophages.

claim: The replication of ΔpanD in RAW264.7 cells decreased 2.4-fold at 20 hr post-infection compared with that of the WT strain.
source: Gentamicin protection assays showed that the replication of ΔpanD in RAW264.7 cells decreased 2.4-fold at 20 hr post-infection compared with that of the WT strain (p<0.001), while complementation of ΔpanD with the panD gene restored the replication ability of the mutant strain in RAW264.7 cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: Complementation of ΔpanD with the panD gene restored the replication ability of the mutant strain in RAW264.7 cells.
source: Gentamicin protection assays showed that the replication of ΔpanD in RAW264.7 cells decreased 2.4-fold at 20 hr post-infection compared with that of the WT strain (p<0.001), while complementation of ΔpanD with the panD gene restored the replication ability of the mutant strain in RAW264.7 cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: The number of ΔpanD in each infected RAW264.7 cell was comparable to that of the WT strain at the initial infection stage (2 hr).
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that the number of ΔpanD in each infected RAW264.7 cell was comparable to that of the WT strain at the initial infection stage (2 hr), but at 20 hr post-infection, the number of ΔpanD in each infected RAW264.7 cell was significantly (p<0.0001) lower than that of the WT strain (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2F and G.

claim: At 20 hr post-infection, the number of ΔpanD in each infected RAW264.7 cell was significantly lower than that of the WT strain.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that the number of ΔpanD in each infected RAW264.7 cell was comparable to that of the WT strain at the initial infection stage (2 hr), but at 20 hr post-infection, the number of ΔpanD in each infected RAW264.7 cell was significantly (p<0.0001) lower than that of the WT strain (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2F and G.

claim: panD contributes to Salmonella replication in macrophages.
source: These results indicate that panD contributes to Salmonella replication in macrophages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gentamicin protection assays and immunofluorescence analysis.

claim: The growth rates of ΔpanD in LB medium and RPMI medium resembled those of the WT.
source: The growth rates of ΔpanD in LB medium and RPMI medium resembled those of the WT (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), indicating that the impaired intracellular replication ability of the mutant was not due to a growth defect.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The impaired intracellular replication ability of the ΔpanD mutant was not due to a growth defect.
source: The growth rates of ΔpanD in LB medium and RPMI medium resembled those of the WT (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), indicating that the impaired intracellular replication ability of the mutant was not due to a growth defect.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the growth curve data.

claim: The replication defect of ΔpanD in RAW264.7 cells was relieved by the addition of 1 mM β-alanine to the RPMI medium.
source: Moreover, the replication defect of ΔpanD in RAW264.7 cells was relieved by the addition of 1 mM β-alanine to the RPMI medium (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2H.

claim: The replication of S. Typhi ΔpanD in human THP-1 macrophages was reduced by 2.6-fold compared to the S. Typhi Ty2 WT strain.
source: We found that the replication of S. Typhi ΔpanD in human THP-1 macrophages was reduced by 2.6-fold compared to the S. Typhi Ty2 WT strain (p<0.01) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting that panD also facilitates S. Typhi replication within human macrophages.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: panD also facilitates S. Typhi replication within human macrophages.
source: We found that the replication of S. Typhi ΔpanD in human THP-1 macrophages was reduced by 2.6-fold compared to the S. Typhi Ty2 WT strain (p<0.01) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting that panD also facilitates S. Typhi replication within human macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing reduced replication of S. Typhi ΔpanD.

claim: β-alanine synthesis is critical for Salmonella replication inside macrophages.
source: These data collectively suggest that β-alanine synthesis is critical for Salmonella replication inside macrophages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing the importance of panD.

claim: Replication in macrophages is a key determinant of systemic Salmonella infection.
source: As replication in macrophages is a key determinant of systemic Salmonella infection, we reasoned that β-alanine synthesis also influences Salmonella systemic infection in vivo.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Salmonella pathogenesis.

claim: β-alanine synthesis influences Salmonella systemic infection in vivo.
source: As replication in macrophages is a key determinant of systemic Salmonella infection, we reasoned that β-alanine synthesis also influences Salmonella systemic infection in vivo.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed importance of β-alanine for intracellular replication.

claim: The WT-infected mice exhibited high lethality and marked loss of body weight within 5 days.
source: The WT-infected mice exhibited high lethality and marked loss of body weight within 5 d, and all mice died within 9 d of infection (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B and C.

claim: All WT-infected mice died within 9 days of infection.
source: The WT-infected mice exhibited high lethality and marked loss of body weight within 5 d, and all mice died within 9 d of infection (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The ΔpanD-infected mice displayed significantly improved survival rates and body weights.
source: In contrast, the ΔpanD-infected mice displayed significantly improved survival rates and body weights, and no mice died within the 10 d surveillance period (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B and C.

claim: No ΔpanD-infected mice died within the 10 day surveillance period.
source: In contrast, the ΔpanD-infected mice displayed significantly improved survival rates and body weights, and no mice died within the 10 d surveillance period (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The bacterial burden in the liver and spleen of the ΔpanD-infected mice was significantly decreased compared with that of the WT-infected mice on day 3 post-infection.
source: Consistent with these results, the bacterial burden in the liver and spleen of the ΔpanD-infected mice was significantly decreased, and the body weight was significantly increased compared with that of the WT-infected mice on day 3 post-infection (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: The body weight of ΔpanD-infected mice was significantly increased compared with that of the WT-infected mice on day 3 post-infection.
source: Consistent with these results, the bacterial burden in the liver and spleen of the ΔpanD-infected mice was significantly decreased, and the body weight was significantly increased compared with that of the WT-infected mice on day 3 post-infection (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Complementation of ΔpanD with panD significantly decreased the survival rate and body weight of infected mice.
source: Complementation of ΔpanD with panD significantly decreased the survival rate and body weight of infected mice but significantly increased the bacterial burden in the liver and spleen of the infected mice (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B-D.

claim: Complementation of ΔpanD with panD significantly increased the bacterial burden in the liver and spleen of the infected mice.
source: Complementation of ΔpanD with panD significantly decreased the survival rate and body weight of infected mice but significantly increased the bacterial burden in the liver and spleen of the infected mice (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B-D.

claim: The bacterial count in each macrophage from ΔpanD-infected mice was significantly lower than that in WT-infected mice, on day 5 post-infection.
source: The results showed that the bacterial count in each macrophage from ΔpanD-infected mice was significantly (P<0.0001) lower than that in WT-infected mice, on day 5 post-infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: Complementation of ΔpanD with panD restored the bacterial count in each macrophage to WT level.
source: Complementation of ΔpanD with panD restored the bacterial count in each macrophage to WT level (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: H&E staining revealed increased aggregation of inflammatory cells and pyknosis in the livers of the WT-infected mice on day 5 post-infection.
source: Furthermore, H&E staining revealed increased aggregation of inflammatory cells and pyknosis in the livers of the WT-infected mice on day 5 post-infection, while these histopathological alterations were obviously reduced in the livers of ΔpanD-infected mice (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: Histopathological alterations were obviously reduced in the livers of ΔpanD-infected mice.
source: Furthermore, H&E staining revealed increased aggregation of inflammatory cells and pyknosis in the livers of the WT-infected mice on day 5 post-infection, while these histopathological alterations were obviously reduced in the livers of ΔpanD-infected mice (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: β-alanine synthesis is critical for systemic Salmonella infection in mice.
source: Taken together, these results reveal that β-alanine synthesis is critical for systemic Salmonella infection in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mouse infection experiments.

claim: Compared with those in the WT strain, 1379 genes were differentially expressed in the ΔpanD strain, with 561 upregulated genes and 618 downregulated genes.
source: Remarkable transcriptional changes were observed due to the mutation of panD. Compared with those in the WT strain, 1379 genes were differentially expressed in the ΔpanD strain, with 561 upregulated genes and 618 downregulated genes (fold change ≥2 and p-value <0.05; Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: The differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were mainly involved in the metabolism and biosynthesis of several amino acids (including arginine, leucine, histidine, and branched amino acids), carboxylic acid metabolism, small molecule biosynthesis, and aerobic respiration.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed that the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were mainly involved in the metabolism and biosynthesis of several amino acids (including arginine, leucine, histidine, and branched amino acids), carboxylic acid metabolism, small molecule biosynthesis, and aerobic respiration (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: KEGG pathway enrichment analysis revealed a high frequency of terms related to metabolism, including amino acid metabolism, lipid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, energy metabolism, and nucleotide metabolism.
source: Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis also revealed a high frequency of terms related to metabolism, including amino acid metabolism, lipid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, energy metabolism, and nucleotide metabolism (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: β-alanine is involved in the regulation of a series of metabolic pathways in Salmonella.
source: These data collectively indicate that β-alanine is involved in the regulation of a series of metabolic pathways in Salmonella.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GO and KEGG enrichment analyses.

claim: Mutation of panD decreased the expression of genes involved in seven pathways that are associated with the virulence of Salmonella or other bacterial pathogens, including methionine metabolism, fatty acid β-oxidation, histidine biosynthesis, and the transport of zinc, galactose, potassium, and polyamine.
source: Further analysis of the downregulated DEGs (activated by PanD) revealed that mutation of panD decreased the expression of genes involved in even pathways that are associated with the virulence of Salmonella or other bacterial pathogens, including methionine metabolism, fatty acid β-oxidation, histidine biosynthesis, and the transport of zinc, galactose, potassium, and polyamine (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Zinc acquisition promotes Salmonella Typhimurium virulence in mice.
source: Zinc and potassium uptake are associated with the virulence of Salmonella (zinc acquisition promotes Salmonella Typhimurium virulence in mice, and potassium acquisition promotes Salmonella Enteritidis virulence in chickens) (Ammendola et al., 2007; Battistoni et al., 2017; Ilari et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2013), while the remaining 5 pathways are involved in the pathogenicity of other pathogens (Basavanna et al., 2013; Paiva et al., 2016; Feldman et al., 2016; Lauriano et al., 2004; Martínez-Guitián et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ammendola et al., 2007; Battistoni et al., 2017; and Ilari et al., 2016.

claim: Potassium acquisition promotes Salmonella Enteritidis virulence in chickens.
source: Zinc and potassium uptake are associated with the virulence of Salmonella (zinc acquisition promotes Salmonella Typhimurium virulence in mice, and potassium acquisition promotes Salmonella Enteritidis virulence in chickens) (Ammendola et al., 2007; Battistoni et al., 2017; Ilari et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2013), while the remaining 5 pathways are involved in the pathogenicity of other pathogens (Basavanna et al., 2013; Paiva et al., 2016; Feldman et al., 2016; Lauriano et al., 2004; Martínez-Guitián et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2013.

claim: The expression of the LysR-type transcriptional regulator LeuO was downregulated in the ΔpanD strain.
source: In addition, the expression of the LysR-type transcriptional regulator LeuO, which activates the expression of the leuABCD leucine synthesis operon and numerous virulence genes in Salmonella Typhimurium (Dillon et al., 2012; Guadarrama et al., 2014; Hernández-Lucas et al., 2008), was also downregulated in the ΔpanD strain (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: LeuO activates the expression of the leuABCD leucine synthesis operon and numerous virulence genes in Salmonella Typhimurium.
source: In addition, the expression of the LysR-type transcriptional regulator LeuO, which activates the expression of the leuABCD leucine synthesis operon and numerous virulence genes in Salmonella Typhimurium (Dillon et al., 2012; Guadarrama et al., 2014; Hernández-Lucas et al., 2008), was also downregulated in the ΔpanD strain (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dillon et al., 2012; Guadarrama et al., 2014; and Hernández-Lucas et al., 2008.

claim: The expression of leuABCD was downregulated in the ΔpanD strain.
source: In line with the decreased expression of leuO, the expression of leuABCD was downregulated in the ΔpanD strain (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: The expression of all 16 selected genes significantly decreased in the ΔpanD mutant compared with the WT strain.
source: The results showed that the expression of all 16 genes significantly (p<0.05) decreased in the ΔpanD mutant compared with the WT strain (Figure 4F), and complementation of ΔpanD with panD restored the gene expression to the WT level (Figure 4F), thus confirming the positive regulation of these pathways and LeuO by β-alanine.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: Complementation of ΔpanD with panD restored the gene expression to the WT level.
source: The results showed that the expression of all 16 genes significantly (p<0.05) decreased in the ΔpanD mutant compared with the WT strain (Figure 4F), and complementation of ΔpanD with panD restored the gene expression to the WT level (Figure 4F), thus confirming the positive regulation of these pathways and LeuO by β-alanine.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: β-alanine positively regulates these pathways and LeuO.
source: The results showed that the expression of all 16 genes significantly (p<0.05) decreased in the ΔpanD mutant compared with the WT strain (Figure 4F), and complementation of ΔpanD with panD restored the gene expression to the WT level (Figure 4F), thus confirming the positive regulation of these pathways and LeuO by β-alanine.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the qRT-PCR data.

claim: SPI-2 gene expression is essential for Salmonella replication in macrophages and systemic infection.
source: SPI-2 gene expression is essential for Salmonella replication in macrophages and systemic infection (Deng et al., 2017), yet the expression of SPI-2 genes was unaffected by panD mutation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Deng et al., 2017.

claim: The expression of SPI-2 genes was unaffected by panD mutation.
source: SPI-2 gene expression is essential for Salmonella replication in macrophages and systemic infection (Deng et al., 2017), yet the expression of SPI-2 genes was unaffected by panD mutation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The gene expression of SPI-1, SPI-3, SPI-4, and SPI-5 is unaffected by panD mutation.
source: Moreover, the gene expression of four other virulence-associated SPIs, SPI-1, SPI-3, SPI-4, and SPI-5, is also unaffected by panD mutation (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: β-alanine might promote Salmonella intracellular replication and virulence by activating virulence-associated pathway(s) or activating the virulence-associated regulator LeuO, rather than by activating the expression of virulence genes encoded within pathogenicity islands.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that β-alanine might promote Salmonella intracellular replication and virulence by activating virulence-associated pathway(s) or activating the virulence-associated regulator LeuO, rather than by activating the expression of virulence genes encoded within pathogenicity islands.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq data showing no effect on SPI gene expression.

claim: Mutations in fadAB, metR, hisABCDFGHL, kdpABC, mglABC, and potFGHI did not influence Salmonella colonization in the mouse liver or spleen.
source: Mouse infection assays revealed that mutations in fadAB, metR, hisABCDFGHL, kdpABC, mglABC, and potFGHI, which are associated with fatty acid β-oxidation, methionine metabolism, histidine biosynthesis, potassium uptake, galactose uptake, and polyamine uptake, respectively, did not influence Salmonella colonization in the mouse liver or spleen (Figure 5A and B) or the body weight of infected mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse infection data presented in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Mutations in fadAB, metR, hisABCDFGHL, kdpABC, mglABC, and potFGHI did not influence the body weight of infected mice.
source: Mouse infection assays revealed that mutations in fadAB, metR, hisABCDFGHL, kdpABC, mglABC, and potFGHI, which are associated with fatty acid β-oxidation, methionine metabolism, histidine biosynthesis, potassium uptake, galactose uptake, and polyamine uptake, respectively, did not influence Salmonella colonization in the mouse liver or spleen (Figure 5A and B) or the body weight of infected mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse infection data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Mutation of the regulatory gene leuO did not influence Salmonella colonization in the mouse liver or spleen.
source: Interestingly, although LeuO has been reported to be associated with the regulation of a diverse set of virulence factors (Dillon et al., 2012; Guadarrama et al., 2014), mutation of the regulatory gene leuO did not influence Salmonella colonization in the mouse liver or spleen (Figure 5A and B) or the body weight of infected mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse infection data presented in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Mutation of the regulatory gene leuO did not influence the body weight of infected mice.
source: Interestingly, although LeuO has been reported to be associated with the regulation of a diverse set of virulence factors (Dillon et al., 2012; Guadarrama et al., 2014), mutation of the regulatory gene leuO did not influence Salmonella colonization in the mouse liver or spleen (Figure 5A and B) or the body weight of infected mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse infection data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Mutation of the zinc transporter gene znuA significantly decreased Salmonella colonization in the mouse liver and spleen.
source: In contrast, mutation of the zinc transporter gene znuA significantly decreased Salmonella colonization in the mouse liver and spleen (Figure 5D, left and middle panels); this result is consistent with previous studies (Ammendola et al., 2007; Battistoni et al., 2017; Ilari et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse infection data presented in Figure 5D and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: The body weight of ΔznuA-infected mice was significantly greater than that of the WT-infected mice.
source: Accordingly, the body weight of ΔznuA-infected mice was significantly (p<0.001) greater than that of the WT-infected mice (Figure 5D, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse infection data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: β-alanine might promote Salmonella virulence in vivo by promoting zinc uptake.
source: These results indicate that β-alanine might promote Salmonella virulence in vivo by promoting zinc uptake.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mouse infection data showing the importance of znuA.

claim: The zinc concentration in the macrophages of ΔpanD-infected mouse livers was 3.2-fold higher than in those of WT-infected mice.
source: We observed that the zinc concentration in the macrophages of ΔpanD-infected mouse livers was 3.2-fold higher than in those of WT-infected mice (p<0.0001; Figure 5E), suggesting that the panD gene and β-alanine are crucial for Salmonella to obtain zinc from host cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: The panD gene and β-alanine are crucial for Salmonella to obtain zinc from host cells.
source: We observed that the zinc concentration in the macrophages of ΔpanD-infected mouse livers was 3.2-fold higher than in those of WT-infected mice (p<0.0001; Figure 5E), suggesting that the panD gene and β-alanine are crucial for Salmonella to obtain zinc from host cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed zinc accumulation in ΔpanD-infected cells.

claim: Colonization of the liver and spleen of infected mice by ΔpanDΔznuA was significantly lower than that of infected mice colonized by ΔznuA.
source: The results showed that colonization of the liver and spleen of infected mice by ΔpanDΔznuA was significantly lower than that of infected mice colonized by ΔznuA (Figure 5D, left and middle panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse infection data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: The body weight of ΔpanDΔznuA-infected mice was greater than that of ΔznuA-infected mice.
source: In agreement with these results, the body weight of ΔpanDΔznuA-infected mice was greater than that of ΔznuA-infected mice (Figure 5D, right panel), suggesting that the contribution of panD to the virulence of Salmonella is partially dependent on znuA.
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse infection data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: The contribution of panD to the virulence of Salmonella is partially dependent on znuA.
source: In agreement with these results, the body weight of ΔpanDΔznuA-infected mice was greater than that of ΔznuA-infected mice (Figure 5D, right panel), suggesting that the contribution of panD to the virulence of Salmonella is partially dependent on znuA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the double mutant data.

claim: β-alanine promotes in vivo virulence of Salmonella partially by increasing the expression of zinc transporter genes.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that β-alanine promotes in vivo virulence of Salmonella partially by increasing the expression of zinc transporter genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mouse infection experiments with the double mutant.

claim: The zinc concentration in ΔpanD-infected RAW 264.7 cells increased by 1.8-fold compared to WT-infected cells.
source: We observed that the zinc concentration in ΔpanD-infected RAW 264.7 cells increased by 1.8-fold compared to WT-infected cells (p<0.0001; Figure 6A), further indicating the panD gene and β-alanine are crucial for Salmonella to absorb zinc from macrophages.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: The panD gene and β-alanine are crucial for Salmonella to absorb zinc from macrophages.
source: We observed that the zinc concentration in ΔpanD-infected RAW 264.7 cells increased by 1.8-fold compared to WT-infected cells (p<0.0001; Figure 6A), further indicating the panD gene and β-alanine are crucial for Salmonella to absorb zinc from macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed zinc accumulation in ΔpanD-infected cells.

claim: The replication of ΔpanDΔznuA in RAW264.7 cells was significantly reduced compared with that of the single mutant ΔznuA.
source: The results showed that the replication of ΔpanDΔznuA in RAW264.7 cells was significantly reduced compared with that of the single mutant ΔznuA (Figure 6B), implying that the contribution of panD to the intracellular replication of Salmonella is partially dependent on znuA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: The contribution of panD to the intracellular replication of Salmonella is partially dependent on znuA.
source: The results showed that the replication of ΔpanDΔznuA in RAW264.7 cells was significantly reduced compared with that of the single mutant ΔznuA (Figure 6B), implying that the contribution of panD to the intracellular replication of Salmonella is partially dependent on znuA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the double mutant data.

claim: The addition of 100 μM zinc to RPMI medium increased the replication of ΔpanD in RAW264.7 cells.
source: The addition of 100 μM zinc to RPMI medium increased the replication of ΔpanD in RAW264.7 cells (Figure 6C), while the addition of 1 mM β-alanine to RPMI medium did not increase the replication of ΔznuA (Figure 6D), suggesting that the impaired replication due to the decrease in β-alanine can be relieved by zinc supplementation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: The addition of 1 mM β-alanine to RPMI medium did not increase the replication of ΔznuA.
source: The addition of 100 μM zinc to RPMI medium increased the replication of ΔpanD in RAW264.7 cells (Figure 6C), while the addition of 1 mM β-alanine to RPMI medium did not increase the replication of ΔznuA (Figure 6D), suggesting that the impaired replication due to the decrease in β-alanine can be relieved by zinc supplementation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: The impaired replication due to the decrease in β-alanine can be relieved by zinc supplementation.
source: The addition of 100 μM zinc to RPMI medium increased the replication of ΔpanD in RAW264.7 cells (Figure 6C), while the addition of 1 mM β-alanine to RPMI medium did not increase the replication of ΔznuA (Figure 6D), suggesting that the impaired replication due to the decrease in β-alanine can be relieved by zinc supplementation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the zinc and β-alanine supplementation experiments.

claim: β-alanine promotes Salmonella replication within macrophages by increasing the expression of zinc transporter genes.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that β-alanine promotes Salmonella replication within macrophages by increasing the expression of zinc transporter genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the macrophage infection experiments.

claim: Salmonella promotes its replication inside macrophages by utilizing both host- and bacterial-derived β-alanine.
source: In this study, we demonstrated that Salmonella promotes its replication inside macrophages by utilizing both host- and bacterial-derived β-alanine (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: β-alanine promotes Salmonella intracellular replication and systemic infection partially by increasing the expression of zinc transporter genes and therefore, the uptake of zinc by intracellular Salmonella.
source: We showed that β-alanine promotes Salmonella intracellular replication and systemic infection partially by increasing the expression of zinc transporter genes and therefore, the uptake of zinc by intracellular Salmonella (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Salmonella relies on a large amount of β-alanine to efficiently replicate in macrophages.
source: We speculate that Salmonella relies on a large amount of β-alanine to efficiently replicate in macrophages, thereby highlighting the importance of β-alanine for Salmonella intracellular growth.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that both host- and bacterial-derived β-alanine are important.

claim: Zinc is an essential micronutrient for all living organisms and is used as a cofactor for various enzymes and proteins.
source: Zinc is an essential micronutrient for all living organisms and is used as a cofactor for various enzymes and proteins (Bock et al., 2016; Ilari et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bock et al., 2016; Ilari et al., 2016; and Tan et al., 2004.

claim: In bacteria, zinc-binding proteins account for approximately 5% of the bacterial proteome and play crucial roles in bacterial metabolism and virulence.
source: In bacteria, zinc-binding proteins account for approximately 5% of the bacterial proteome and play crucial roles in bacterial metabolism and virulence (Andreini et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Andreini et al., 2006.

claim: Knockout of the zinc transporter ZnuABC reduces the virulence of Salmonella, Campylobacter jejuni, Haemophilus ducreyi, Moraxella, and urinary tract pathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) in the host.
source: Knockout of the zinc transporter ZnuABC reduces the virulence of Salmonella, Campylobacter jejuni, Haemophilus ducreyi, Moraxella, and urinary tract pathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) in the host (Ilari et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ilari et al., 2016.

claim: Zinc is utilized by Salmonella to subvert the antimicrobial host defense of macrophages by inhibiting NF-кB activation and impairing NF-кB-dependent bacterial clearance.
source: Moreover, zinc is also utilized by Salmonella to subvert the antimicrobial host defense of macrophages by inhibiting NF-кB activation and impairing NF-кB-dependent bacterial clearance (Jennings et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2017).

claim: Salmonella utilizes the high-affinity ZnuABC zinc transporter to optimize zinc availability in host cells.

claim: β-alanine can increase the expression of the zinc transporter genes znuABC, which could represent an additional mechanism for the efficient zinc uptake of Salmonella in macrophages.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased znuABC expression with β-alanine.

claim: The utilization of β-alanine promotes Salmonella uptake of the essential micronutrient zinc, which was previously shown to be required for the metabolic needs of intracellular Salmonella and to subvert the antimicrobial defense of macrophages by Salmonella.
source: We propose that Salmonella requires a large amount of β-alanine during intracellular infection. The utilization of β-alanine promotes Salmonella uptake of the essential micronutrient zinc, which was previously shown to be required for the metabolic needs of intracellular Salmonella and to subvert the antimicrobial defense of macrophages by Salmonella.
evidence: This is a summary of the proposed model based on the study's findings and previous knowledge.

claim: The panD gene is present in the genomes of all Salmonella strains.
source: Considering that the panD gene is present in the genomes of all Salmonella strains and that mutation of panD markedly reduced Salmonella replication ability in macrophages, as well as virulence in the mouse model, this gene may be used as a potential target to control systemic Salmonella infection.
evidence: This is stated as a consideration for the potential application of the findings.
